Aviation communication links aircraft, controllers, airline operations, and automated systems. It combines highly responsive voice channels for tactical control with datalink systems for structured messages, oceanic operations, and routine operational exchanges.


Aviation communication is essential for maintaining safe and efficient air traffic management. Two main types of communication systems are used: **voice communication**, which remains the primary method for controller–pilot interaction, and **data communication**, which increasingly supports operational efficiency through digital message exchange.

## Voice communications

The most widely used system for voice communication is **\acr{VHF}** radio, operating between $118$ and $137~\mathrm{MHz}$ with amplitude modulation (AM). \acr{VHF} provides reliable, line-of-sight communication over ranges of up to about $200~\mathrm{nm}$, which is sufficient for most continental airspaces. It is fast, clear, and highly responsive, making it ideal for air traffic control in busy regions such as Europe. However, the limited available spectrum required a progressive reduction of channel spacing, from $50~\mathrm{kHz}$ to $25~\mathrm{kHz}$ and today to $8.33~\mathrm{kHz}$, allowing more frequencies to be allocated in dense airspaces.

<!-- Line of Sight -->
::: {.callout-tip}
#### Example: Line-of-sight propagation

**\acr{VHF}** radio waves propagate approximately in straight lines and therefore do not follow the curvature of the Earth. The maximum communication range is consequently limited by the **radio horizon** of the transmitter and receiver. For a transmitter or receiver at height $h$ above the Earth's surface, the distance to the horizon can be approximated by

$$
d \approx \sqrt{2Rh},
$$

where $R$ is the radius of the Earth. For communication between an aircraft at height $h_\mathrm{h_1}$ and a ground station at height $h_\mathrm{h_2}$, the approximate maximum line-of-sight distance is therefore

$$
d_\mathrm{max} \approx \sqrt{2R} \cdot (\sqrt{\mathrm{h_1}} + \sqrt{\mathrm{h_2}}) 
$$

**Example.** Consider an aircraft flying at $\mathrm{h_1}=35\,000~\mathrm{ft} \approx 10.67~\mathrm{km}$) and a \acr{VHF} ground antenna located $\mathrm{h_2}=30~\mathrm{m}$ above the surrounding terrain. Using an Earth radius of $R = 6\,371~\mathrm{km}$ gives

$$
d_\mathrm{max} \approx \sqrt{2 \cdot 6\,371} \cdot (\sqrt{\mathrm{10.67}} + \sqrt{\mathrm{0.03}}) 
\approx
389~\mathrm{km}
\approx
210~\mathrm{nm}.
$$

Thus, even with sufficient transmitter power, communication with this ground station will normally become impossible once the aircraft moves much beyond about $210~\mathrm{nm}$ because the Earth itself blocks the direct propagation path.

:::

For long-haul flights over oceans and other remote areas, \acr{HF} radio is used. \acr{HF} signals reflect off the ionosphere, enabling communication across thousands of kilometers where \acr{VHF} coverage is not possible. The system is less reliable than \acr{VHF} because signal quality depends on solar activity, time of day, and atmospheric conditions. Communication may be lost temporarily, and the audio quality is often poor. To reduce the burden on pilots, who would otherwise need to monitor the noisy channels continuously, \acr{SELCAL} is used: each aircraft has a unique code, and only when addressed by \acr{ATC} does the cockpit receive an audible alert.

In procedural or non-radar airspace, pilots also provide \acr{AIREP}. These reports contain position, weather observations, turbulence, and other relevant data and are transmitted to \acr{ATC} or Flight Information Services via voice, typically over \acr{VHF} or \acr{HF}. \acr{AIREP} are an important complement to radar surveillance and remain vital in oceanic and remote regions.

## Data communications

Alongside voice, **data communication systems** play an increasingly important role. Datalink is not a single radio system: it is a layered architecture in which operational applications use one or more communication bearers. The same aircraft may exchange messages through classic \acr{VHF} ACARS, \acr{VDL} Mode 2, \acr{HFDL}, or \acr{SATCOM}, depending on region, equipage, and operational need.

The historically central system is **\acr{ACARS}**, introduced for short operational messages between aircraft and ground systems. ACARS is best understood as a common message service that can carry many kinds of aviation communication: airline operations messages, maintenance reports, weather requests, departure clearances, oceanic clearances, position reports, and some air traffic services messages. Public ACARS aggregation projects such as [airframes.io](https://docs.airframes.io/docs/intro/) illustrate the breadth of these applications; the detailed message formats are discussed later in the data-source chapters.

## Operational applications

Some datalink applications support airline operations rather than direct air traffic control.

A common example is **\acr{OOOI}** reporting: aircraft automatically send timestamps for out, off, on, and in events, corresponding roughly to leaving the gate, take-off, landing, and arriving at the gate. Airlines use these messages for flight following, punctuality monitoring, crew and passenger information, and downstream operational planning.

Other **\acr{AOC}** messages may carry fuel requests, gate information, load sheets, maintenance reports, diversion information, or free text.

Other applications support air traffic services. **\acr{CPDLC}** enables controllers to send non-time-critical clearances and instructions directly to the cockpit display, and enables pilots to respond using structured message elements. It reduces frequency congestion and avoids some readback/hearback errors, but it does not replace voice for urgent tactical instructions. In Europe, \acr{CPDLC} is mandatory for many aircraft above FL285 and is based on \acr{VDL} Mode 2. Over the North Atlantic and other remote regions, \acr{CPDLC} is often provided through \acr{FANS} 1/A using VHF or satellite communication depending on availability.

**\acr{ADS-C}** is also part of the communication picture. Unlike \acr{ADS-B}, which broadcasts position reports to anyone in range, \acr{ADS-C} is contract based: an \acr{ATSU} and an aircraft agree what information should be sent and under which conditions. This makes it especially useful in oceanic and remote airspace, where radar and ground-based \acr{ADS-B} coverage may be limited.

## Communication performance

To ensure safety in non-radar-controlled environments, **\acr{PBC}** introduces quantitative requirements. The key concept is **\acr{RCP}**, which specifies the maximum time allowed for a complete communication transaction, from controller instruction to pilot acknowledgment. For example, RCP 240 requires that 99.9% of transactions be completed within 240 seconds. These standards allow aircraft separation to be reduced safely even in areas where communication delays are expected.

In summary, modern aviation communication integrates both **voice** and **data systems**. Voice remains essential for time-critical control, while datalink systems improve efficiency, reduce workload, and support operations far beyond terrestrial radio coverage. Together, they ensure robust communication across continental, oceanic, and remote operations.
